ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure shows a series-regulated voltage-stabilized power supply. The upper-left end is an unregulated input labeled 15V(UR), which goes through the upper series transistor Q1 to the output terminal Vout on the right. On the left there is a 1 kΩ resistor connected from the 15 V input to a node, and this node is connected to the + input of the op-amp; this node is also grounded through a Zener diode labeled 6V, thereby forming a 6 V reference. The output terminal on the right is connected to a voltage-divider network composed of 12 kΩ and 24 kΩ in series, with 12 kΩ on top and 24 kΩ below and grounded, and the midpoint of the two feeds back to the - input of the op-amp. A 10 Ω load to ground is also drawn at the output terminal, and the ground symbol is an inverted triangle. Then reason: Under ideal regulator conditions, the op-amp adjusts Q1 so that the negative-feedback divider-point voltage equals the 6 V Zener reference voltage at the + input terminal. The divider-point voltage is Vout × 24 kΩ / (12 kΩ + 24 kΩ). Therefore 6 = Vout × 24 / 36 = (2/3)Vout, giving Vout = 9 V. Q1 is connected in series between the 15 V input and the 9 V output, so the voltage drop across Q1 is 15 - 9 = 6 V. According to the answer convention given in this problem, fill the blank with 6 W.
